name: Wood-Filled PLA
chemical_makeup: PLA matrix loaded with real wood particulate/fibre, commonly cited at 20-40 wt% (about 30 % typical); the fibre is lower-density than the resin, so the composite ends up slightly lighter than base PLA
summary: PLA compounded with real wood fibre for a sandable, wood-look, wood-smelling part. Versus base PLA it needs a hardened nozzle, slower speeds (40-60 mm/s) and more retraction, is lighter (1.21 vs 1.24 g/cm³), and is much weaker and more anisotropic (tensile XY 26 MPa, Z 15 MPa vs 45-65 MPa base). It is also the worst of the six aesthetic variants outdoors, because the fibre absorbs water independently of the PLA.

printing.notes: Deltas vs base PLA: hardened nozzle, slower speeds, and nozzle diameter matters. Bambu's TDS gives 190-240 °C and rates the material below 250 mm/s, but community practice is 40-60 mm/s, dropping further as fibre load rises, to avoid fibre packing and clogs. Darker/higher-fibre shades generally run hotter within the range; nozzle temperature also controls how much the fibre 'toasts', which is how colour variegation is dialled in. Use 0.4 mm or larger (0.6/0.8 mm preferred for heavily filled shades) — fibre bridges small orifices. Bambu's own TDS does not state a hardened-nozzle requirement, but wood fibre visibly abrades brass within roughly 12-48 h of continuous printing per community reports, so this entry flags it as required.

feeding.notes: Feeds through Bowden or direct drive, but increase retraction over your base-PLA profile (~5 mm Bowden, 0.5-1 mm direct drive) because fibre content makes flow start and stop less cleanly. Bambu's material table lists wood/rock-filled PLA as AMS-compatible only 'when not very brittle, rough, or soft' — darker high-fibre shades can be brittle enough to snap in the feed path and rough enough to wear PTFE, so this is 'conditional' and batch-dependent. No feeding assistant needed (rigid).

drying.dryness_validation: Listen for steam pops and watch for rough, spitting extrusion on a purge line — wood-PLA announces moisture far more loudly than base PLA. Surface finish is a poor indicator here because the material is intentionally rough.
drying.notes: Bambu specifies 55 °C for 8 h, essentially base-PLA drying; community guidance runs 45-60 °C for 4-6 h. The important delta is not the schedule but the consequence — the wood fibre takes up moisture independently of the PLA matrix, so an under-dried spool causes steam pops and flow disruption much sooner than base PLA would.

storage.recommendations: Drybox with desiccant is worth the effort here even though base PLA tolerates open air — the fibre fraction keeps absorbing moisture after the PLA has stabilised

price.notes: Bambu PLA Wood around $24.99/kg — a moderate premium over base PLA at $18-20/kg, in line with pla-gradient and pla-glow

recommended: parts intended to be sanded, stained or finished like wood
props where a wood grain look and smell sells the piece
not_recommended: parts loaded in Z (Z tensile is roughly half XY)
fine thin walls or 0.2 mm nozzle detail work (fibre clogs)
unsealed outdoor use (fibre swells and degrades)

properties.notes: Bambu PLA Wood TDS: density 1.21 g/cm³ — lower than base PLA's 1.24 despite added filler, because wood fibre is less dense than the resin, making this the lightest of the six aesthetic variants. Tensile XY 26±5 MPa and Z 15±4 MPa (a Z/XY ratio near 0.58, the worst in this cluster), elongation XY 15.3±3.1 % and Z 4.5±1.7 %, Tg 54 °C, HDT 57 °C at 1.8 MPa. Important product-category caution: this entry describes particle-filled wood PLA. Chemically foamed 'wood-look' PLA is a different product with density near 0.8 g/cm³ — these numbers do not apply to it.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and to base PLA, though the fibre-roughened melt surface makes PLA-to-wood interfaces slightly less reliable than PLA-to-PLA — keep multi-material seams out of load paths. Not listed as usable support for anything: the rough, fibre-loaded surface leaves a poor interface finish on the supported part, unlike base PLA which is a good breakaway support for PETG.

plate_recommendations.notes: Adheres well at 35-45 °C and the plate texture is cosmetically irrelevant against an intentionally rough wood-look surface. Choose smooth PEI instead when the bottom face will be sanded flat and finished.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): As base PLA; wood-filled blends are specifically listed as compatible.

alternatives.reason: When the wood look is not essential, base PLA is dramatically stronger (tensile XY 45-65 vs 26 MPa, adh 6 vs 3), runs at full speed with no hardened nozzle (ease 10 vs 6) and costs less ($14-35 vs $24-26).

The mineral sibling on the same ease 6 filled-PLA terms: denser and grittier, takes paint and patina like cast stone, and behaves better in damp air (water 5 vs 3, weath 2 vs 1) since there is no fibre to wick — but it is heavy (1.70 vs 1.21 g/cm³) and cannot be sanded to grain.
If what you actually want is a non-plastic, layer-line-hiding surface to paint: ease 9 vs 6, no hardened nozzle, no extra retraction tuning, and much better strength and bonding (adh 5 vs 3).

Wood-fill is the worst aesthetic PLA outdoors (weath 1, water 3); for planters, garden markers or anything that gets wet, PETG survives (water 9, weath 5, temp 5 vs 2) — at the total loss of the wood grain and smell, and ease 7 vs 6.

emissions.notes: The one emissions delta in this cluster: fibre charring at the nozzle produces a distinct burnt-wood smell that is normal but can be strong in a small closed room, and adds particulate beyond base PLA's baseline. Not classified as hazardous, but move air rather than printing it on a desk in an unventilated space.

safety_notes: Wear a mask when sanding — wood-PLA dust is a mix of wood and plastic fines. The composite is not food-contact certified and no supplier guarantees the fibre feedstock is free of contaminants.
additional_notes: Nozzle temperature doubles as a colour control: hotter extrusion toasts the fibre darker, so deliberately varying temperature by height produces grain-like variegation. Parts sand, stain and wax like soft wood, which is the main reason to accept the mechanical penalty.

provenance.conflicts: Magnitude of embrittlement is genuinely disputed: Bambu's TDS reports elongation XY 15.3 %, while a secondary community composite dataset reports elongation at break of only ~3.8 % (vs ~9.4 % for base PLA), tensile modulus ~3650 MPa vs ~2700 MPa, and flexural strength collapsing to ~14 MPa. These are almost certainly different fibre loadings; treat exact numbers as brand- and fill-percentage-dependent and the datasheet values as applying to Bambu's product only. Fibre content itself is unpublished by Bambu (20-40 wt% is a secondary-source figure). Hardened nozzle: flagged required here on community evidence (brass wear in ~12-48 h of continuous printing, hours unverified) even though Bambu's TDS does not state it. Warp is reported by some sources as slightly better than base PLA because fibre restrains shrinkage — unverified, so warp is recorded equal to base PLA at 1.

trade_names.notes: Wood-fill under the PLA+/Pro label; pla-plus not additionally asserted since no toughening spec is published for the wood grade.
